title: Removing an item from a Spell defers it rather than rejecting it, because removals land in the Executive Vote queue
content:
Two provisions close a loop. A.1.10.2.4.3.1.3: "Content being removed from the Executive Sheet is added to the Executive Vote queue to be included in the next Executive Vote cycle." A.1.10.2.4.1.2.1: the Governance Point "must review the Executive Vote queue, which contains items that were included in the previous cycle(s) but removed from the Executive Sheet" and decide which to include now.

So removal is not a decision about merit at all — it is a scheduling operation on a persistent backlog that the next cycle is obliged to read.

This is what makes the risk-driven removals elsewhere in the process politically survivable. If removal meant rejection, every request to strip a Spell would be a fight with whoever sponsored the item, and Crafters would face social pressure to accept an overloaded Spell. Because the item provably returns, the Crafter's request costs the sponsor a week rather than the outcome.

More generally, this separates two decisions that governance processes often fuse: *whether* something should happen (settled by the governance path that put it on the sheet) and *when* it can be safely executed (settled per-cycle by risk and review capacity). Keeping them separate lets the second be decided freely and often, without reopening the first.
description: The queue is a first-class content source reviewed at Step 1 of the next cycle, which is what makes it cheap for a Spell Crafter to strip a Spell down on risk grounds.
